findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing, conflating failure with empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing (src/store.go:10) when the key is absent. LoadOrDefault discards that error with `v, _ := Load(...)` and returns "". But "" is also what Load legitimately returns for a key that exists with an empty value (Load returns v, nil @src/store.go:12). The two states are therefore indistinguishable at the boundary of an exported API: every caller is forced to treat a genuine lookup failure as a real value (and vice versa), which is exactly the failure-vs-value conflation Trigger D targets. This is a present defect in the public contract, not speculation about a future caller.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing, conflating absent key with empty value

LoadOrDefault drops the error with `v, _ :=` and returns "" for both cases, so every caller is forced to treat a missing key as if it were a real, present empty value. A caller validating presence, defaults, or persistence cannot detect the failure path at all, and this is an exported API contract defect independent of any current in-repo caller.

findings.title: Log's new tag parameter is silently ignored
findings.whyItBreaks: The signature gained `tag ...string`, implying emitted output is tagged, but the body still only calls `println(message)` and never references `tag`. Go neither errors nor warns on an unused parameter, so a future caller doing `logger.Log("user deleted", "audit")` accepts the call, sees no error, and gets untagged output indistinguishable from a call that passed no tag. The public signature is the contract, and it promises behavior the body does not implement; the tag signal is dropped with no compile-time or runtime indication.

findings.title: clampPercent name promises clamping but body never clamps
findings.whyItBreaks: The rename toPercent -> clampPercent (a public export) asserts behavior the body does not implement: Math.round((done/total)*100) returns values outside [0,100] whenever done > total (e.g. clampPercent(150,100) === 150) or done < 0 (e.g. clampPercent(-5,100) === -5). The caller progressBar trusts the implied clamp and passes pct into String.repeat: "#".repeat(pct) throws RangeError for negative pct and "-".repeat(100 - pct) throws RangeError for pct > 100, so an exported API now advertises a guarantee that produces a crash instead of a clamped result.

findings.title: clampPercent never clamps, crashing progressBar on out-of-range input
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported symbol is renamed `clampPercent`, a name whose contract is a capped percentage in [0,100], but the body still computes the raw `Math.round((done/total)*100)` with no clamping. `progressBar` (src/progress.ts:6) relies on that promise: it feeds `pct` into `"#".repeat(pct)` and `"-".repeat(100 - pct)`, and `String.prototype.repeat` throws `RangeError: Invalid count value` for a negative count. So any caller trusting the name—e.g. `progressBar(150, 100)` (pct=150 → `"-".repeat(-50)`) or a negative `done` (negative `"#".repeat`)—crashes instead of producing a clamped bar.

findings.title: recentEntries drops the `limit` cap, returning the whole feed
findings.whyItBreaks: The body was changed from `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)` to `const sorted = [...all].reverse(); if (limit <= 0) return []; return sorted;`, so for any `limit > 0` the limit is never applied and the full reversed array is returned. The unchanged carrier on line 1 still promises "Returns at most `limit` entries, newest first", and the only caller `renderFeed` (line 9) relies on the cap: it calls `recentEntries(all, 20)` and copies `page.length` entries, so a feed with more than 20 entries now renders every entry (the `out` array starting at length 20 is extended by out-of-range writes) instead of a 20-entry page. Note that the added `limit <= 0` guard is redundant (`slice(0, limit)` already yielded `[]`), so the only real change is the lost cap.
